summary: Describes the RTP payload format for the Enhanced Variable Rate Codec and the Selectable Mode Vocoder, both speech codecs. Two sub-formats are given, including a bundled and interleaved one that reduces the effect of packet loss. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3558 defines Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) payload formats for EVRC and SMV speech frames. It offers single-frame and bundled or interleaved formats to balance delay, bandwidth, and packet loss.

questions: rtp payload format for evrc and smv
what is interleaving in rtp audio
subtitle: How to pack frames from two CDMA speech codecs into RTP packets, with optional bundling and interleaving to survive packet loss.

tldr.problem: The EVRC and SMV speech codecs produce small frames every 20 milliseconds, and RTP needs a standard way to carry them, ideally one that hides packet loss and saves header overhead.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two packet formats: an interleaved/bundled format with a small payload header and a table of contents, and a header-free format that carries a single frame.
tldr.outcome: A sender can pick low latency or loss resilience per application. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 4788.

today: RFC 3558 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2003 and has been updated by RFC 4788. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3558 describes how speech compressed with EVRC (Enhanced Variable Rate Codec) or SMV (Selectable Mode Vocoder) is formatted as an RTP payload. The format can also be reused for other codecs that produce a similar set of frame types.

Two methods are provided: an interleaved/bundled format and a header-free (zero-header) format. The sender chooses the best one for each application, based on network conditions, bandwidth, delay requirements and tolerance of packet loss.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines two ways to put EVRC or SMV speech frames into RTP packets. The sender chooses the format based on delay, bandwidth, and tolerance for lost packets.

sections.title: The Two Codecs
sections.content:
Both codecs come from the 3rd Generation Partnership Project 2 (3GPP2) and were designed for CDMA mobile systems. Each takes 20 milliseconds of 8000 Hz, 16-bit sampled speech and produces one output frame whose size depends on the speech and the operating mode.

EVRC frames come in three sizes: Rate 1 (171 bits), Rate 1/2 (80 bits) and Rate 1/8 (16 bits). SMV adds Rate 1/4 (40 bits) and can run in six modes, switchable frame by frame. Both also have two zero-bit frame types: null frames (the codec ran at rate 0) and erasure frames (substituted by the receiver for lost or damaged frames). Neither is normally transmitted.

Other frame-based vocoders can use this format if they are frame-based, support blank and erasure frames, have fewer than 17 rates, and fit a full-rate frame in one RTP packet.
sections.plainLanguage: EVRC and SMV produce speech frames every 20 milliseconds. The frame size depends on the codec rate, and some frame types carry no speech bits.

sections.title: Two Packet Formats
sections.content:
In the interleaved/bundled format, the RTP header is followed by one octet holding two reserved bits (RR), a 3-bit interleave length (LLL) and a 3-bit interleave index (NNN). A second octet holds a 3-bit Mode Request (MMM) and a 5-bit frame Count. The number of frames is the Count value plus one, so one to 32 frames fit in a packet. After that comes one 4-bit table-of-contents (ToC) entry per frame, then 4 bits of padding if the frame count is odd, then the codec data frames.

The RTP timestamp is in 1/8000 of a second units for EVRC and SMV. With several frames in a packet, the timestamp is that of the oldest data.

In the header-free format, there are no payload header fields and no ToC. The packet holds exactly one codec data frame, and its rate is inferred from its length. It is meant for maximum bandwidth efficiency and low latency.

All receivers SHOULD handle both formats. A receiver MUST know the format in advance, and if both are used in one session they MUST use different payload type values, agreed out of band, for example with SDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The bundled format carries a small header, a table of contents, and one or more speech frames. The header-free format carries exactly one frame and lets the receiver infer its rate from its length.

sections.title: ToC Entries and Codec Data Frames
sections.content:
Each ToC entry is a 4-bit frame type. For EVRC and SMV the values are fixed: 0 blank, 1 Rate 1/8, 2 Rate 1/4, 3 Rate 1/2, 4 Rate 1, and 5 erasure. Values not listed are reserved, and an entry with a reserved value SHOULD be treated as invalid. Value 2 is also reserved when EVRC is in use, because EVRC has no quarter-rate frames.

Codec output bits are packed into octets with the lowest-numbered bit in the most significant bit of the first octet. Any unused bits in the last octet MUST be zero. Only Rate 1 needs this: 171 bits become a 22-octet frame with 5 padding bits. The other rates fit whole octets, at 2, 5 and 10 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each table-of-contents entry identifies the frame type and size. The sender packs frame bits into octets and sets unused final bits to zero.

sections.title: Interleaving and Bundling
sections.content:
Bundling puts several consecutive frames in one packet so the RTP and payload header cost is shared. Interleaving goes further: it spreads frames across packets so that a lost packet removes non-adjacent frames. The codecs can cover for an occasional lost frame, but speech quality degrades exponentially with consecutive losses.

Bundling is signalled by LLL equal to 0 with a Count above zero. A value of LLL above zero means interleaving. An interleave group is LLL plus 1 packets with sequential sequence numbers, and every packet in a group MUST have the same bundling value. Packets in a group MUST be sent in increasing NNN order. An invalid NNN (greater than LLL) means the packet SHOULD be ignored.

Receivers can limit the work with two optional parameters set at session start: maxptime (default 200 milliseconds) and maxinterleave (default 5). Senders MUST NOT exceed them, MAY change the interleave value only between groups, and MUST use silence suppression only between groups. Inside a group, a blank frame (type 0) is used instead.

For interactive use, the RFC recommends an interleave length of 0 or the header-free format. When delay is not the main concern, an interleave length of 4 or 5 is a reasonable compromise.
sections.plainLanguage: Bundling puts several frames in one packet, reducing repeated header cost. Interleaving spreads nearby frames across packets so one lost packet is less likely to remove consecutive speech frames.

sections.title: Missing Frames, Late Packets and Mode Requests
sections.content:
A receiver uses the sequence number, timestamp and marker bit to notice missing frames and feeds the decoder an erasure frame for each, so the decoder advances by one frame time. The decoder then interpolates, and quality is best when erasures are not consecutive. A packet with invalid ToC fields or a length mismatch is RECOMMENDED to be discarded and treated as lost. If a late packet arrives before its next frame is needed, the receiver should use the frames from it rather than an erasure.

The 3-bit Mode Request field asks the other end to switch its encoder mode, and so the bit rate of the reverse stream. It SHOULD be used only in one-to-one sessions and ignored in multi-party ones. A node SHOULD keep sending the same value until it wants a different mode, so one lost packet cannot leave the codec stuck. Its meaning for EVRC and SMV comes from the codec specifications.

A storage format for files or e-mail attachments starts with a magic number (#!EVRC\n or #!SMV\n) and stores each frame with its ToC entry widened to one octet. Lost frames MUST be stored as erasure frames.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver uses RTP sequence numbers and timestamps to detect missing frames and supplies erasure frames to the decoder. The mode request field can ask the other endpoint to change its encoder mode.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The format inherits the security considerations of RTP and its profile. Confidentiality comes from encryption, and because compression is end-to-end, encryption can be applied after compression. The RFC notes that these codecs do not have the uneven decoding cost that would make a pathological-packet denial of service easy.

A receiver can still be overloaded by too many packets. Interleaving may also affect encryption: depending on the scheme, a key change may need to happen at the boundary between interleave groups.
sections.plainLanguage: The format follows RTP’s security requirements. Encryption can protect the compressed media, but an encryption key change may need to wait until an interleave group ends.
